topic: Systems of Two Linear Equations in Two Variables

lesson.intro: A system of two linear equations asks a single question: is there a point $(x, y)$ that satisfies both equations at once? Graphically that point is where two lines cross. The Digital SAT tests three things about such systems -- solving them quickly by substitution or elimination, recognising when a system has no solution or infinitely many, and building a system from a short story about tickets, prices, speeds or mixtures. Every one of those tasks is worth practising until it is automatic, because systems appear on both modules of every test.

blocks.title: What a solution is
blocks.body:
A solution to a system such as
\[\begin{cases}2x + y = 7\\x - y = 2\end{cases}\]is an ordered pair $(x, y)$ that makes \emph{both} equations true. Here $(3, 1)$ works: $2(3)+1 = 7$ and $3-1 = 2$. Because each equation graphs as a line, the solutions of the system are exactly the points the two lines share. Two distinct lines either cross once, or never cross (they are parallel), or coincide completely -- which is why a linear system has one solution, no solution, or infinitely many, and never exactly two.

Checking a candidate pair is always legitimate: substitute it into both equations. If it satisfies only one, it is not a solution.

blocks.title: Method 1 -- substitution
blocks.body:
Substitution is the right tool when one equation is already solved for a variable, or when a variable has coefficient $1$ so isolating it costs nothing.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Solve one equation for one variable.
\item Substitute that expression into the \emph{other} equation. You now have one equation in one variable.
\item Solve it, then substitute back to get the second variable.
\end{enumerate}

Substituting back into the equation you just came from returns a true but useless statement such as $7 = 7$; always go back to the other equation.

blocks.title: Worked example -- substitution
blocks.body:
Solve \[\begin{cases}y = 3x - 4\\2x + y = 11\end{cases}\]

The first equation is already solved for $y$, so replace $y$ in the second equation:
\[2x + (3x - 4) = 11 \;\Longrightarrow\; 5x - 4 = 11 \;\Longrightarrow\; 5x = 15 \;\Longrightarrow\; x = 3.\]
Now substitute $x = 3$ into $y = 3x - 4$: $y = 9 - 4 = 5$. The solution is $(3, 5)$.

Check it in the equation that was not used for the back-substitution: $2(3) + 5 = 11$. True, so the pair is correct.

blocks.title: Method 2 -- elimination
blocks.body:
Elimination is faster when both equations are in the form $ax + by = c$. Add or subtract multiples of the equations so that one variable cancels.

\begin{enumerate}
\item Multiply one or both equations so that the coefficients of one variable are equal in size and opposite in sign.
\item Add the equations; that variable disappears.
\item Solve for the survivor, then substitute back.
\end{enumerate}

When you multiply an equation, multiply \emph{every} term, including the constant on the right.

blocks.title: Worked example -- elimination
blocks.body:
Solve \[\begin{cases}4x + 3y = 18\\5x - 2y = 11\end{cases}\]

To cancel $y$, scale the first equation by $2$ and the second by $3$:
\[\begin{aligned}
8x + 6y &= 36\\
15x - 6y &= 33
\end{aligned}\]
Adding gives $23x = 69$, so $x = 3$. Substituting into $4x + 3y = 18$ gives $12 + 3y = 18$, so $y = 2$. The solution is $(3, 2)$.

Notice that the choice to eliminate $y$ was deliberate: its coefficients $3$ and $-2$ already had opposite signs, so the scaled equations could simply be added.

blocks.title: How many solutions?
blocks.body:
Write both equations as $a_1x + b_1y = c_1$ and $a_2x + b_2y = c_2$ and compare the three ratios.

\begin{itemize}
\item $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \neq \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}$: the slopes differ, the lines cross once -- \textbf{exactly one solution}.
\item $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$: same slope, different intercept -- \textbf{no solution}.
\item $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$: one equation is a multiple of the other -- \textbf{infinitely many solutions}.
\end{itemize}

In slope-intercept form the same rules read: different slopes give one solution; equal slopes with different $y$-intercepts give none; identical equations give infinitely many.

blocks.title: The facts to memorise
blocks.body:
For the system $a_1x + b_1y = c_1$ and $a_2x + b_2y = c_2$:
\[\text{one solution} \iff a_1b_2 - a_2b_1 \neq 0.\]
When $a_1b_2 = a_2b_1$ the lines are parallel; they coincide only if the constants scale by the same factor.
\[\text{no solution} \iff \frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \frac{c_1}{c_2}, \qquad \text{infinitely many} \iff \frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{c_1}{c_2}.\]

blocks.title: Answering the wrong question
blocks.body:
The single most common way to lose a system question is to solve it perfectly and then report the wrong number. If you find $x = 3$ and $y = 5$, the test may ask for $y$, for $x + y$, for $2x - y$, or for the price of one shirt \emph{and} one hat. Every one of $3$, $5$, $8$ and $1$ will be sitting in the answer choices.

Underline what is being asked before you start, and write both coordinates down before you look at the choices. A second trap: when a question asks for $x + y$ or $x - y$, adding or subtracting the two equations often produces it in one line, so check for that shortcut before grinding out both variables.

blocks.title: Choosing a method, and using the calculator
blocks.body:
Scan the system first.

\begin{itemize}
\item A variable already isolated, or a coefficient of $1$: \textbf{substitute}.
\item Matching or opposite coefficients: \textbf{eliminate}.
\item Coefficients swapped between the equations, as in $4x + 7y$ and $7x + 4y$: add for $x+y$, subtract for $x-y$.
\item Fractions or decimals: multiply through to clear them \emph{before} doing anything else.
\end{itemize}

On the Bluebook Desmos calculator you can type both equations and read the intersection point straight off the graph -- fast and reliable for messy numbers. For questions with a parameter such as $k$, algebra is still faster than graphing, because the ratio test answers them in one line.

blocks.title: Building a system from words
blocks.body:
Nearly every SAT system word problem has two unknowns and two facts. One fact usually counts objects and the other counts money, distance or amount.

\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Tickets}: $a + c = \text{total tickets}$ and $12a + 8c = \text{total dollars}$.
\item \emph{Mixture}: $x + y = \text{total volume}$ and $0.10x + 0.30y = \text{total acid}$.
\item \emph{Two plans}: set the two cost expressions equal to find when they match.
\item \emph{Upstream and downstream}: the effective speeds are $b + c$ and $b - c$.
\end{itemize}

Define your variables in writing, with units. "$a$ = number of adult tickets" prevents the wrong-variable error at the end.

blocks.title: Worked example -- a word problem
blocks.body:
A shop sells notebooks for $\$4$ and folders for $\$3$. A customer buys $10$ items and pays $\$34$. How many notebooks did the customer buy?

Let $n$ be the number of notebooks and $f$ the number of folders. Counting items gives $n + f = 10$; counting money gives $4n + 3f = 34$. Substituting $f = 10 - n$:
\[4n + 3(10 - n) = 34 \;\Longrightarrow\; n + 30 = 34 \;\Longrightarrow\; n = 4.\]
So the customer bought $4$ notebooks and $6$ folders. Check: $4(4) + 3(6) = 16 + 18 = 34$.

The structure is worth remembering: if all $10$ items were folders the bill would be $\$30$, and each notebook adds $\$1$ to that baseline, so the $\$4$ excess means $4$ notebooks.

problems.stem: In the system shown, what is the value of $x$?\[\begin{cases}y = 2x\\3x + y = 20\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: The first equation already gives $y$ in terms of $x$, so substitution is the fastest route: replacing $y$ by $2x$ turns a two-variable system into a one-variable equation. Once $x=4$ is known, $y=8$ follows, but the question asked only for $x$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(y, 2*x), Eq(3*x + y, 20)], [x, y])
result = sol[x]

problems.stem: What is the value of $x$ in the system below?\[\begin{cases}x + y = 10\\x - y = 4\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: When the same variable appears with opposite coefficients, adding the equations eliminates it in one line. The $y$ terms cancel, leaving $2x = 14$. The value $3$ is $y$, the variable the question did not ask about.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(x + y, 10), Eq(x - y, 4)], [x, y])
result = sol[x]

problems.stem: If $x + y = 12$ and $2x + y = 17$, what is the value of $y$?
problems.solution: Subtracting the first equation from the second removes $y$ immediately, because both equations carry exactly one $y$. That gives $x=5$, and back-substitution gives $y=7$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(x + y, 12), Eq(2*x + y, 17)], [x, y])
result = sol[y]

problems.stem: The system below has exactly one solution $(x, y)$. What is the value of $y$?\[\begin{cases}y = x + 3\\y = 2x - 1\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: Two expressions equal to the same $y$ must be equal to each other. Setting them equal gives $x=4$; substituting back into either equation gives $y=7$. Stopping at $x=4$ is the standard error here.
steps: Set the two expressions for $y$ equal: $x + 3 = 2x - 1$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(y, x + 3), Eq(y, 2*x - 1)], [x, y])
result = sol[y]

problems.stem: For the solution $(x, y)$ of the system shown, what is the value of $x + y$?\[\begin{cases}4x + y = 17\\y = x + 2\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: The SAT often asks for a combination rather than for a single variable. Solve the system fully, then build what was asked: $x=3$ and $y=5$ give $x+y=8$. Answering $3$ or $5$ means answering a question that was not posed.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(4*x + y, 17), Eq(y, x + 2)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] + sol[y]

problems.stem: What is the value of $y$ in the system below?\[\begin{cases}2x + y = 7\\3x - y = 8\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: The coefficients of $y$ are $+1$ and $-1$, so adding the equations kills $y$ at once and gives $x=3$. The question, though, asks for $y$: substitute back to get $y = 7 - 6 = 1$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(2*x + y, 7), Eq(3*x - y, 8)], [x, y])
result = sol[y]

problems.stem: A theater sells adult tickets for $\$12$ each and child tickets for $\$8$ each. On one evening the theater sold $24$ tickets and collected $\$232$. How many adult tickets were sold?
problems.solution: Two unknowns need two equations: one counting tickets and one counting dollars. The count equation is the easy one to substitute with, since $c = 24 - a$ has no fractions.
steps: Let $a$ be adult tickets and $c$ child tickets: $a + c = 24$ and $12a + 8c = 232$.
problems.verify:
a, c = symbols('a c')
sol = solve([Eq(a + c, 24), Eq(12*a + 8*c, 232)], [a, c])
result = sol[a]

problems.stem: What is the value of $y$ in the system below?\[\begin{cases}3x + 2y = 16\\5x - 4y = -10\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: Neither variable cancels as written, so scale first: doubling the top equation makes the $y$ coefficients $+4$ and $-4$. Adding then gives $x = 2$, and substituting back gives $y = 5$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(3*x + 2*y, 16), Eq(5*x - 4*y, -10)], [x, y])
result = sol[y]

problems.stem: If $2x - 3y = 5$ and $4x + 3y = 19$, what is the value of $x + y$?
problems.solution: The $y$ coefficients are already opposites, so no scaling is needed: adding gives $6x = 24$. Solve for both variables and then form the requested sum.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(2*x - 3*y, 5), Eq(4*x + 3*y, 19)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] + sol[y]

problems.stem: The ordered pair $(x, y)$ is the solution to the system shown. What is the value of $2x - y$?\[\begin{cases}3x + 2y = 19\\x - 2y = -7\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: Adding eliminates $y$ and gives $x = 3$; back-substitution gives $y = 5$. The requested expression is $2x - y = 6 - 5 = 1$. Choice D is what you get if you compute $2x + y$ instead.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(3*x + 2*y, 19), Eq(x - 2*y, -7)], [x, y])
result = 2*sol[x] - sol[y]

problems.stem: For what value of $k$ does the system below have infinitely many solutions?\[\begin{cases}kx + 6y = 10\\2x + 3y = 5\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: Infinitely many solutions means the two equations describe the same line, so one must be a constant multiple of the other. Comparing the $y$ terms, $6 = 2 \cdot 3$, and the constants agree as well, $10 = 2 \cdot 5$; so the multiplier is $2$ and $k = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$.
steps: For one line to be a multiple of the other, compare $y$ terms: $6 \div 3 = 2$.
Check the constants: $10 \div 5 = 2$, the same multiplier.
So the $x$ terms must also match: $k = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$.
problems.verify:
k = symbols('k')
result = solve(Eq(k/2, S(6)/3), k)[0]

problems.stem: The system below has no solution. What is the value of $k$?\[\begin{cases}6x + ky = 9\\2x + 5y = 4\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: No solution means parallel but distinct lines: the coefficients are proportional while the constants are not. From $6 \div 2 = 3$ the multiplier is $3$, so $k = 3 \cdot 5 = 15$; and since $9 \neq 3 \cdot 4$, the lines really are distinct.
steps: For parallel lines the $y$ terms must scale the same way: $k = 3 \cdot 5 = 15$.
Check the constants: $3 \cdot 4 = 12 \neq 9$, so there is indeed no solution.
problems.verify:
k = symbols('k')
result = solve(Eq(S(6)/2, k/5), k)[0]

problems.stem: At a school store a pen costs $\$2$ and a notebook costs $\$5$. Maria buys $12$ items in total and pays $\$39$. How many notebooks does she buy?
problems.solution: Let $p$ and $n$ be the numbers of pens and notebooks. The count equation $p + n = 12$ substitutes cleanly into the cost equation. Notice the answer $7$ is the number of pens: label your variables before you answer.
problems.verify:
p, n = symbols('p n')
sol = solve([Eq(p + n, 12), Eq(2*p + 5*n, 39)], [p, n])
result = sol[n]

problems.stem: Two cars start at the same time from points $300$ miles apart and drive toward each other along a straight road. They meet after $3$ hours. One car travels $20$ miles per hour faster than the other. What is the speed, in miles per hour, of the faster car?
problems.solution: In $3$ hours the two cars together cover $300$ miles, so the sum of their speeds is $100$ mph. With the difference of the speeds given as $20$, the sum-and-difference system solves in one step. Choice A is the slower car.
problems.verify:
r, s = symbols('r s')
sol = solve([Eq(r + s, 100), Eq(r, s + 20)], [r, s])
result = sol[r]

problems.stem: If $5x + 2y = 2$ and $3x - 2y = 14$, what is the value of $x - y$?
problems.solution: The $y$ terms are already opposites, so adding gives $8x = 16$ and $x = 2$. Then $y = -4$, and the requested difference is $2 - (-4) = 6$ -- subtracting a negative is where this item is usually lost.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(5*x + 2*y, 2), Eq(3*x - 2*y, 14)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] - sol[y]

problems.stem: What is the value of $y$ in the system below?\[\begin{cases}\frac{x}{2} + \frac{y}{3} = 4\\x - y = 3\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: Clear the fractions first: multiplying by the common denominator $6$ turns the top equation into $3x + 2y = 24$. Then substitute $x = y + 3$ to get $5y + 9 = 24$, so $y = 3$ and $x = 6$. Choice B is $x$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(x/2 + y/3, 4), Eq(x - y, 3)], [x, y])
result = sol[y]

problems.stem: If $4x + 7y = 17$ and $7x + 4y = 27$, what is the value of $x + y$?
problems.solution: When the coefficients are swapped between the two equations, adding them produces a multiple of $x + y$ directly -- no need to find $x$ and $y$ separately. Here $11x + 11y = 44$, so $x + y = 4$. Choice D is the sum before dividing by $11$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(4*x + 7*y, 17), Eq(7*x + 4*y, 27)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] + sol[y]

problems.stem: The system $ax + 4y = 10$ and $3x + 6y = 12$ has no solution. What is the value of $a$?
problems.solution: Parallel distinct lines have equal slopes. Matching the ratio of the $x$ terms to the ratio of the $y$ terms gives $a/3 = 4/6$, so $a = 2$; the constants $10$ and $12$ are not in that same ratio, which is exactly why no solution exists.
steps: Check: $\dfrac{10}{12} \neq \dfrac{2}{3}$, so the lines are parallel and distinct.
problems.verify:
a = symbols('a')
result = solve(Eq(a/3, S(4)/6), a)[0]

problems.stem: A chemist mixes a $10\%$ acid solution with a $30\%$ acid solution to make $20$ liters of a $25\%$ acid solution. How many liters of the $30\%$ solution are used?
problems.solution: One equation tracks total volume and the other tracks total acid. The acid equation is $0.10x + 0.30y = 0.25(20) = 5$. Solving gives $x = 5$ and $y = 15$; choice A is the amount of the weak solution, the classic wrong-variable trap.
steps: Let $x$ and $y$ be the liters of $10\%$ and $30\%$ solution: $x + y = 20$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(x + y, 20), Eq(S(1)/10*x + S(3)/10*y, 5)], [x, y])
result = sol[y]

problems.stem: Which of the following statements about the system $2x - 5y = 8$ and $-4x + 10y = -16$ is true?
choices: The system has exactly one solution.
The system has exactly two solutions.
The system has infinitely many solutions.
problems.solution: Multiplying the first equation by $-2$ reproduces the second equation exactly, so the two equations graph as the same line and every point on it is a solution. A system of two linear equations can never have exactly two solutions, which rules out choice C outright.
steps: That is precisely the second equation.
The equations describe one line, so every point on it solves the system.

problems.stem: If $5x + 3y = 29$ and $3x + 5y = 27$, what is the value of $x - y$?
problems.solution: Subtracting the second equation from the first gives $2x - 2y = 2$, which is $2(x-y)$. The combination the question asks for appears without ever computing $x$ or $y$ on their own -- always check whether the requested expression is a shortcut away.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(5*x + 3*y, 29), Eq(3*x + 5*y, 27)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] - sol[y]

problems.stem: For what value of $c$ does the system below have infinitely many solutions?\[\begin{cases}4x - 6y = 10\\-2x + 3y = c\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: The first equation is $-2$ times the left side of the second, so the two are the same line only when the constants obey the same factor: $10 = -2c$, giving $c = -5$. Forgetting the negative sign produces choice C.
steps: The same multiplier must work on the constants: $10 = -2c$.
problems.verify:
c = symbols('c')
result = solve(Eq(c/10, S(-2)/4), c)[0]

problems.stem: The system shown has solution $(x, y)$. What is the value of $x + y$?\[\begin{cases}y = 4x - 1\\y = 2x + 7\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: Both equations are solved for $y$, so set the right sides equal: $4x - 1 = 2x + 7$ gives $x = 4$ and then $y = 15$. The question asks for the sum, $19$; choices A and B are the individual coordinates.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(y, 4*x - 1), Eq(y, 2*x + 7)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] + sol[y]

problems.stem: What is the value of $y$ in the system below?\[\begin{cases}2x + 5y = 19\\4x - 5y = -7\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: The $y$ coefficients are exact opposites, so adding the equations eliminates $y$ and gives $x = 2$. Substituting back gives $5y = 15$, so $y = 3$; choice A is $x$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(2*x + 5*y, 19), Eq(4*x - 5*y, -7)], [x, y])
result = sol[y]

problems.stem: A concert sold student tickets for $\$9$ each and adult tickets for $\$15$ each. A total of $40$ tickets were sold for $\$456$. How many adult tickets were sold?
problems.solution: Substituting $s = 40 - a$ into the money equation is the efficient move: the $\$9$ baseline accounts for $\$360$, and every adult ticket adds $\$6$ more than a student ticket does.
steps: Let $s$ and $a$ be student and adult tickets: $s + a = 40$.
problems.verify:
s, a = symbols('s a')
sol = solve([Eq(s + a, 40), Eq(9*s + 15*a, 456)], [s, a])
result = sol[a]

problems.stem: If $(x, y)$ satisfies $7x + 3y = 27$ and $2x + 3y = 12$, what is the value of $2x - y$?
problems.solution: Both equations carry $3y$, so subtracting removes $y$ at once: $5x = 15$. With $x = 3$ and $y = 2$, the requested expression is $6 - 2 = 4$. Choice D is $2x + y$, the sign-slip answer.
steps: Subtract the second equation from the first: $5x = 15$, so $x = 3$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(7*x + 3*y, 27), Eq(2*x + 3*y, 12)], [x, y])
result = 2*sol[x] - sol[y]

problems.stem: The system $8x + ky = 12$ and $2x + 5y = 7$ has no solution. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: No solution means the lines are parallel, so the coefficients scale by the same factor: $8 \div 2 = 4$ forces $k = 4 \cdot 5 = 20$. Since $12 \neq 4 \cdot 7$, the lines are distinct, confirming there is truly no solution.
steps: Apply the same factor to the $y$ terms: $k = 4 \cdot 5 = 20$.
Check the constants: $4 \cdot 7 = 28 \neq 12$, so the lines never meet.
problems.verify:
k = symbols('k')
result = solve(Eq(S(8)/2, k/5), k)[0]

problems.stem: The graphs of $y = -2x + 9$ and $y = x - 3$ intersect at the point $(x, y)$. What is the value of $x + 2y$?
problems.solution: An intersection point is exactly a solution of the system, so set the two expressions for $y$ equal. That gives $x = 4$ and $y = 1$, so $x + 2y = 6$. Choice A is $x$ alone and choice B is $x + y$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(y, -2*x + 9), Eq(y, x - 3)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] + 2*sol[y]

problems.stem: A bakery sells muffins for $\$3$ each and scones for $\$4$ each. One morning it sold $25$ of these items for a total of $\$87$. How many muffins did it sell?
problems.solution: If all $25$ items were muffins the total would be $\$75$; each scone adds $\$1$, so there were $12$ scones and therefore $13$ muffins. Choice C is the number of scones -- the count the question did not ask for.
steps: Let $m$ and $s$ be muffins and scones: $m + s = 25$ and $3m + 4s = 87$.
problems.verify:
m, s = symbols('m s')
sol = solve([Eq(m + s, 25), Eq(3*m + 4*s, 87)], [m, s])
result = sol[m]

problems.stem: What is the value of $y$ in the system below?\[\begin{cases}0.5x + 0.2y = 2.6\\x - y = 1\end{cases}\]
problems.solution: Multiply the first equation by $10$ to clear decimals: $5x + 2y = 26$. Substituting $x = y + 1$ gives $7y + 5 = 26$, so $y = 3$ and $x = 4$. Choice C is $x$; choice D is $x + y$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(S(1)/2*x + S(1)/5*y, S(13)/5), Eq(x - y, 1)], [x, y])
result = sol[y]

problems.stem: If $5x + 4y = 6$ and $3x + 2y = 4$, what is the value of $x - y$?
problems.solution: Doubling the second equation matches its $y$ term to the first, so subtracting eliminates $y$ and leaves $x = 2$. Then $y = -1$, and $x - y = 2 - (-1) = 3$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(5*x + 4*y, 6), Eq(3*x + 2*y, 4)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] - sol[y]

problems.stem: In the system $2x + 3y = 7$ and $6x + 9y = c$, $c$ is a constant. For what value of $c$ does the system have infinitely many solutions?
problems.solution: The second left side is exactly $3$ times the first, so the equations agree only when the constants share that factor: $c = 3 \cdot 7 = 21$. For any other $c$ the lines are parallel and there is no solution at all.
steps: Since $2x + 3y = 7$, the second equation reads $3(7) = c$.
problems.verify:
c = symbols('c')
result = solve(Eq(c/7, S(6)/2), c)[0]

problems.stem: A museum charges $\$8$ for an adult ticket and $\$5$ for a child ticket. On Saturday it sold $90$ tickets and collected $\$600$. How many child tickets were sold?
problems.solution: If all $90$ tickets were child tickets the museum would collect $\$450$; each adult ticket adds $\$3$, so $150 \div 3 = 50$ adults and $40$ children. Choice D is the number of adults.
steps: Let $a$ and $c$ be adult and child tickets: $a + c = 90$ and $8a + 5c = 600$.
problems.verify:
a, c = symbols('a c')
sol = solve([Eq(a + c, 90), Eq(8*a + 5*c, 600)], [a, c])
result = sol[c]

problems.stem: If $4x + y = 13$ and $2x + 3y = 9$, what is the value of $3x + 2y$?
problems.solution: Solve the system once, then assemble the requested expression. Substituting $y = 13 - 4x$ gives $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, so $3x + 2y = 9 + 2 = 11$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(4*x + y, 13), Eq(2*x + 3*y, 9)], [x, y])
result = 3*sol[x] + 2*sol[y]

problems.stem: Gym A charges a $\$40$ registration fee plus $\$15$ per month. Gym B charges a $\$10$ registration fee plus $\$20$ per month. After how many months will the two gyms have cost the same total amount?
problems.solution: Write a cost equation for each gym and set them equal -- the point where two linear models agree is the solution of the system. The $\$30$ head start of Gym B is erased at $\$5$ per month, so it takes $6$ months.
problems.verify:
m, C = symbols('m C')
sol = solve([Eq(C, 40 + 15*m), Eq(C, 10 + 20*m)], [m, C])
result = sol[m]

problems.stem: If $3(x + y) = 15$ and $2x - y = 4$, what is the value of $2y - x$?
problems.solution: Divide the first equation by $3$ to get the far friendlier $x + y = 5$; adding it to $2x - y = 4$ gives $3x = 9$. With $x = 3$ and $y = 2$, the requested value is $4 - 3 = 1$. Choice D is $2y + x$.
steps: Divide the first equation by $3$: $x + y = 5$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(3*(x + y), 15), Eq(2*x - y, 4)], [x, y])
result = 2*sol[y] - sol[x]

problems.stem: A boat travels $24$ miles downstream in $2$ hours and the same $24$ miles upstream in $3$ hours. What is the speed of the current, in miles per hour?
problems.solution: Downstream the current helps and upstream it hinders, so the effective speeds are $b + c$ and $b - c$. Those come to $12$ and $8$ mph, a sum-and-difference system whose solution is $b = 10$, $c = 2$.
problems.verify:
b, c = symbols('b c')
sol = solve([Eq(b + c, 12), Eq(b - c, 8)], [b, c])
result = sol[c]

problems.stem: The system $ax + 5y = 12$ and $4x + 10y = 7$ has no solution, where $a$ is a constant. What is the value of $a$?
problems.solution: Parallel lines need proportional coefficients: $a/4 = 5/10$, so $a = 2$. The constants must not follow that ratio, and indeed $12/7 \neq 1/2$. Choice D comes from doubling the wrong equation.
steps: Check: $\dfrac{12}{7} \neq \dfrac{1}{2}$, so the lines are parallel and distinct.
problems.verify:
a = symbols('a')
result = solve(Eq(a/4, S(5)/10), a)[0]

problems.stem: The system $3x + ky = 8$ and $6x + 10y = 16$ has infinitely many solutions, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Every part of the second equation is twice the corresponding part of the first: $6 = 2 \cdot 3$ and $16 = 2 \cdot 8$. For the equations to be identical, $10$ must equal $2k$, so $k = 5$. Choice C is the coefficient copied without halving it.
steps: Compare the constants: $16 \div 8 = 2$, the same factor.
problems.verify:
k = symbols('k')
result = solve(Eq(S(3)/6, k/10), k)[0]

problems.stem: The sum of two numbers is $34$. Three times the larger number exceeds twice the smaller number by $62$. What is the larger number?
problems.solution: Translate each sentence into an equation: $x + y = 34$ and $3x - 2y = 62$, where $x$ is the larger. Substituting $y = 34 - x$ gives $5x = 130$, so $x = 26$ and $y = 8$. Choice A is the smaller number.
steps: Let $x$ be the larger and $y$ the smaller: $x + y = 34$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(x + y, 34), Eq(3*x - 2*y, 62)], [x, y])
result = sol[x]

problems.stem: If $7x + 5y = 31$ and $5x + 7y = 17$, what is the value of $x - y$?
problems.solution: With the coefficients swapped, subtracting the equations gives $2x - 2y = 14$, so $x - y = 7$ without ever isolating a variable. Choice A is $x + y$, which comes from adding instead; choice D is the difference before dividing by $2$.
steps: Subtract the second equation from the first: $2x - 2y = 14$.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
sol = solve([Eq(7*x + 5*y, 31), Eq(5*x + 7*y, 17)], [x, y])
result = sol[x] - sol[y]

problems.stem: The system $y = 5x + 2$ and $y = (k - 1)x - 3$ has no solution, where $k$ is a constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Two lines in slope-intercept form miss each other exactly when their slopes match but their intercepts do not. Setting $k - 1 = 5$ gives $k = 6$, and since $-3 \neq 2$ the lines really are parallel rather than identical.
steps: The intercepts $2$ and $-3$ differ, so the system has no solution.
problems.verify:
k = symbols('k')
result = solve(Eq(k - 1, 5), k)[0]

problems.stem: In the system $2x - y = 4$ and $6x - 3y = c$, $c$ is a constant. For what value of $c$ does the system have at least one solution?
problems.solution: Since $6x - 3y = 3(2x - y)$ and $2x - y = 4$, the second equation is forced to read $c = 12$. For any other value the two lines are parallel and the system has no solution at all, so $12$ is the only value that permits a solution.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y')
result = simplify((6*x - 3*y).subs(y, 2*x - 4))

problems.stem: At a shop, $3$ shirts and $2$ hats cost $\$85$, and $2$ shirts and $5$ hats cost $\$75$. What is the total cost, in dollars, of one shirt and one hat?
problems.solution: Let $s$ and $h$ be the two prices. Elimination gives $s = 25$ and $h = 5$, so a shirt and a hat together cost $\$30$. Choices B and C are the individual prices; the question asks for their sum.
steps: Multiply the first by $5$ and the second by $2$: $15s + 10h = 425$ and $4s + 10h = 150$.
problems.verify:
s, h = symbols('s h')
sol = solve([Eq(3*s + 2*h, 85), Eq(2*s + 5*h, 75)], [s, h])
result = sol[s] + sol[h]
